subject: English
name: English, Year 9
placeName: Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory

points.title: Language that gives power
points.brief: Word choices such as titles, technical terms, commands and the inclusive we can give a speaker authority or make others feel part of a group.

points.title: Direct and indirect evaluation
points.brief: A writer can judge openly, such as calling a plan foolish, or indirectly, through hints, comparisons and loaded words that lead the reader to a view.

points.title: Allusion
points.brief: An allusion is a brief reference to a well-known person, story or event, such as calling a hard task a marathon, which brings that meaning into the text.

points.title: Evocative vocabulary
points.brief: Evocative words call up strong pictures and feelings, such as trudged instead of walked, and quietly carry the writer's judgement.

points.title: Subverting text conventions
points.brief: Authors sometimes break the usual structure of a genre, such as starting a story at the end, to surprise readers or make a point.

points.title: Combining modes in multimodal texts
points.brief: Multimodal texts combine words, images, sound and movement, and each mode adds meaning the others cannot.

points.title: Cohesion through pronouns and word chains
points.brief: Pronouns that refer back, and chains of related words, link sentences so a text reads as one connected whole.

points.title: Connectives that build an argument
points.brief: Connectives such as furthermore, in contrast, therefore and despite this show how each idea adds to, opposes or follows from the last.

chapters.title: Language for expressing and developing ideas

points.title: Sentence fragments for effect
points.brief: A sentence fragment, or a dependent clause standing alone, breaks the usual rules on purpose to create emphasis, drama or a conversational voice.

points.title: Abstract nouns
points.brief: Abstract nouns name ideas and qualities, such as freedom or injustice, and they let a writer sum up a whole situation in one word.

points.title: Connotation and denotation
points.brief: Denotation is a word's dictionary meaning. Connotation is the feeling it carries, so slim and skinny mean much the same but feel different.

points.title: Vocabulary, mood and tone
points.brief: Word choices build the mood a reader feels and the tone, or attitude, the writer takes, such as playful, bitter or formal.

points.title: Punctuation for quoting and citing
points.brief: Quotation marks show borrowed words, an ellipsis shows words left out, square brackets show words changed, and a citation says where the words came from.

chapters.title: Literature and contexts, and responding to literature

points.title: Representation of people and places
points.brief: A representation is how a text portrays a person, group or place, and it is always shaped by the creator's choices and context.

points.title: Representation in First Nations Australian literature
points.brief: First Nations Australian authors represent their own peoples, Country and histories, often challenging earlier representations made by others.

points.title: Personal response that develops
points.brief: A strong personal response compares first impressions of a text with what closer study of the whole text reveals.

points.title: Why readers prefer certain texts
points.brief: Features such as genre, pace, characters readers care about and a distinctive voice explain why some texts appeal to particular readers.

points.title: Evaluating literary style
points.brief: Readers judge an author's style by how well its features, such as sentence rhythm, imagery and voice, suit the text's purpose and appeal to readers.

points.title: Extended metaphor
points.brief: An extended metaphor carries one comparison through several lines or a whole text, such as treating life as a journey with roads and crossroads.

points.title: Metonymy
points.brief: Metonymy names something by a thing closely linked to it, such as the crown for a king or queen, or Canberra for the federal government.

points.title: Allegory
points.brief: An allegory is a story whose characters and events stand for ideas or real events, so it carries a second, deeper meaning.

points.title: Symbolism in literature
points.brief: A symbol is an object, colour or setting that stands for an idea, such as a dove for peace, and it can gather meaning across a text.

points.title: Symbols in film and images
points.brief: Still and moving images use symbols, such as a broken clock or a closing door, to add meaning without words.

chapters.title: Texts in context and interacting with others

points.title: Representation in media texts
points.brief: News stories and advertisements represent people, places and events in ways that reflect the values and context of their makers.

points.title: How speakers position listeners
points.brief: Speakers use tone, emotive words, anecdotes and direct address to lead listeners to respond in a particular way.

points.title: Representing a perspective
points.brief: A text shows a perspective through what it includes, what it leaves out and the words it uses, which can reveal bias.

points.title: Paragraph organisation and meaning
points.brief: Where an author places an idea, such as first for impact or last to leave a lasting impression, changes its effect on the reader.

points.title: Comparing texts
points.brief: Comparing two texts means finding how they treat the same idea alike and differently, and explaining why.

points.title: Fact, opinion and claims
points.brief: A fact can be checked, an opinion is a view, and a claim presented as fact still needs evidence before readers accept it.

points.title: Writing critically
points.brief: Critical writing questions a text or idea, looking at whose views it serves and whose it leaves out, rather than just describing it.

points.title: Creating hybrid texts
points.brief: Students can create hybrid literary texts, such as a story told through texts and photos, choosing structures and features to suit the audience.

points.title: Structuring a speech
points.brief: A speech opens with a hook, signposts its main points, develops them with examples and closes with a memorable ending.

points.title: Spelling for effect
points.brief: Writers bend spelling on purpose to show an accent, a character's way of speaking or humour, while standard spelling stays the norm.
